summary: Specifies the Time Zone Information Format (TZif) for representing and exchanging time zone information independent of any particular service or protocol, and defines two media types. It obsoletes RFC 8536.

plainLanguage.summary: Clocks in different places show different times, and the difference changes when daylight saving rules change. TZif is the standard binary file format in which UNIX systems record those rules, so any program can read them. This RFC describes the format, adds a new version for leap-second tables that expire, and replaces RFC 8536.

subtitle: The compact binary file format that UNIX systems use to store time zone offsets, daylight saving rules and leap seconds.

tldr.problem: Software needs a shared way to describe a place's UT offsets, daylight saving transitions, zone abbreviations and leap seconds, independent of any one service or protocol.
tldr.mechanism: TZif is a binary file: a 44-octet header, a data block of transition times and local time types, and (from version 2) a 64-bit second copy plus a footer holding a POSIX-style TZ string for future times.
tldr.outcome: It documents the widely deployed format, adds version 4 for leap-second table truncation and expiry, defines two media types, and obsoletes RFC 8536.

today: RFC 9636 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8536, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What TZif Is For
sections.content:
Time zone data typically consists of offsets from universal time (UT), daylight saving transition rules, one or more local time designations (acronyms or abbreviations), and optional leap-second adjustments. One other format for conveying this information is iCalendar (RFC 5545), a text-based format used by calendaring and scheduling systems.

This document specifies the widely deployed Time Zone Information Format (TZif). It is a binary format used by most UNIX systems to calculate local time. The format was introduced in the 1980s and has evolved into multiple upward-compatible versions. A wide variety of interoperable software generates and reads files in this format.

The specification does not define the source of the data assembled into a TZif file. One such source is the IANA-hosted time zone database, maintained as described in RFC 6557. The RFC obsoletes RFC 8536, keeping full compatibility with that interchange format while adding editorial improvements, new details, errata fixes and a new format version.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers need to know how the local clock relates to universal time, and how that relationship changes over the year. TZif is the standard file format for storing those rules, and most UNIX systems already use it. The RFC describes the format and replaces an earlier specification.

sections.title: File Layout and Versions
sections.content:
A TZif file begins with a fixed 44-octet version 1 header, followed by a version 1 data block that uses four-octet (32-bit) times. These 32-bit values only cover time changes from 1901-12-13 20:45:52 through 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UT, so the version 1 part exists only for backward compatibility with obsolescent readers.

Files of version 2 and higher append a second 44-octet header, a data block with eight-octet (64-bit) times, and a footer. The 64-bit values can represent times approximately 292 billion years into the past or future. Version 1 files terminate after the version 1 data block.

Readers designed for version N can read version N+1 files without too much trouble: data specific to version N+1 either appears after version N data, so earlier readers can skip it, or appears as a minor extension that version N readers are likely to tolerate. All multi-octet integers are stored big-endian (network octet order), and signed values use two's complement.

The version octet distinguishes the editions. Version 1 is marked with NUL. Version 2 requires a footer whose TZ string follows the POSIX TZ rules, with leap-second records neither truncated nor expired. Version 3 allows a TZ string extension. Version 4 allows leap-second records to be truncated at the start and to carry an expiration time.
sections.plainLanguage: The file starts with a short edition that old programs can read, then a longer edition with wider time values and a rule for future times. Each part begins with its own header, so a program can skip the part it does not need. A version number in the header tells the program which rules the file may use.

sections.title: The TZif Header
sections.content:
Each header starts with the four-octet magic TZif (0x54 0x5A 0x69 0x66) and a one-octet version, then 15 reserved octets, then six four-octet counts: isutcnt, isstdcnt, leapcnt, timecnt, typecnt and charcnt. The counts say how many UT/local indicators, standard/wall indicators, leap-second records, transition times, local time type records and designation octets follow in the data block.

The version octet MUST be NUL (version 1), 2, 3 or 4. typecnt and charcnt MUST NOT be zero, because many readers reject files with zero time types. isutcnt and isstdcnt MUST each be zero or equal to typecnt. The version 1 and version 2+ headers share a format, but their counts may differ because the version 1 data can be a subset of the version 2+ data.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a fixed-size block at the start of each part of the file. It names the format, gives the version number, and lists how many items of each kind the data block contains. A reader uses these counts to find where each list starts and ends.

sections.title: The Data Block
sections.content:
A data block consists of seven variable-length elements, in this order: transition times, transition types, local time type records, time zone designations, leap-second records, standard/wall indicators and UT/local indicators. Each element's length is its item count times its item size, so a reader that does not want the version 1 data can compute its total length and skip directly to the version 2+ header.

Transition times are strictly ascending UNIX leap time values; each SHOULD be at least -2^59. Each transition has a one-octet type index into the local time type records, which are six octets each: a four-octet signed utoff (seconds to add to UT, SHOULD be in [-89999, 93599]), a one-octet DST flag (0 or 1), and a one-octet index into the NUL-terminated designation strings. A designation of -00 marks the time type as a placeholder meaning local time is unspecified.

The type for a transition governs timestamps from that transition up to, but not including, the next one. Timestamps before the first transition use time type 0. Leap-second records pair an occurrence time with a correction value (LEAPCORR), sorted in ascending order; each leap second occurs at the end of a UTC month. In version 4 files, the last two records MAY share a correction value, in which case the last occurrence marks the expiration time of the leap-second table. The standard/wall and UT/local indicator arrays record whether each type's transition times were written as UT, standard time or wall-clock time.
sections.plainLanguage: The data block holds two short lists: the moments when the rules change, and the clock styles (for example winter time and summer time) that take effect. Each moment points at the style to use. Optional records describe leap seconds, and small flag arrays say how the transition times were written.

sections.title: The Footer and TZ Strings
sections.content:
The footer, present only in version 2 and higher, is an ASCII newline, a TZ string and another newline. The TZ string is a rule for computing local time after the last stored transition. It is either empty, meaning the information is not available, or it uses the expanded POSIX TZ format in ASCII. If it is non-empty and transitions exist, it MUST agree with the last transition: evaluating the string at that time must yield the same time type.

Version 3 files MAY use an extension in which the hours part of a transition time may be signed and range from -167 through 167, instead of POSIX's unsigned 0 through 24. For example, <-03>3<-02>,M3.5.0/-2,M10.5.0/-1 describes daylight saving from 22:00 the day before March's last Sunday until 23:00 the day before October's last Sunday. A file that uses this extension MUST be version 3 or higher.

The RFC also spells out all-year daylight saving time: DST is in effect all year if its UT offset is less than (west of) standard time's, and it runs from January 1 at 00:00 until December 31 at 24:00 minus the difference between the two offsets, leaving no room for standard time. Its example is XXX3EDT4,0/0,J365/23, a zone perpetually 4 hours west of UT and abbreviated "EDT".
sections.plainLanguage: After the list of past clock changes runs out, a short rule in the footer describes what happens next, such as jumping ahead in spring and back in autumn. That rule uses the same syntax as the standard POSIX TZ environment variable, with one extension for transitions an hour before or after the usual day boundary.

sections.title: Writing and Reading Safely
sections.content:
Writers SHOULD NOT generate version 1 files, because they cannot represent times after 2038. Other than that, writers SHOULD use the lowest version number the data needs: a version 4 file only if the leap-second table expires or is truncated at the start, and a version 3 file only if the TZ string extension is needed to model transitions accurately. To save space, writers of version 2+ files MAY output a placeholder version 1 block with all counts zero except typecnt and charcnt set to one.

Time zone designations MUST be three to six ASCII characters drawn from alphanumerics, the hyphen and the plus sign. A reader that meets anything else SHOULD act as if the designation were a signed numeric string derived from the UT offset, such as -10 or +0530. Readers of version 2+ files SHOULD ignore the version 1 header and data block except to skip them, and SHOULD check that the computed lengths of headers and data blocks fit the actual file size.

When a leap-second table expiration time is present, readers SHOULD either refuse post-expiration timestamps or process them as if the expiration did not exist, possibly with an error. Appendix A lists common bugs in older readers: some read only version 1 data, some mishandle timestamps after the last transition, some cannot parse the TZ string extension, some mishandle daylight saving offsets smaller than standard time (as in Ireland), and some mishandle UT offsets outside -12 through +12 hours. The RFC also notes that translating abbreviations for other languages is the reader's job; abbreviations are ambiguous, and the Unicode CLDR time zone charts are one approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple rules keep files readable by many programs: use the simplest version that holds the data, keep zone abbreviations short and plain ASCII, and check the file is as long as its own counts say. The RFC also lists known bugs in older readers and how writers can work around them.

sections.title: Media Types and TZDIST
sections.content:
Section 9 registers two media types: application/tzif for files without leap-second records (where leapcnt MUST be zero) and application/tzif-leap for files that include leap-second records as necessary. Both share the same magic number and are intended for widespread use by tools such as the Time Zone Information Compiler (zic) and the GNU C Library.

A Time Zone Data Distribution Service (TZDIST, RFC 7808) MAY serve TZif. If it does, it MUST list application/tzif in its capabilities response, and it MUST NOT advertise application/tzif-leap without also advertising application/tzif. Clients MUST use the HTTP Accept header field to state which format they want.

A TZDIST service MAY truncate data. When truncating the start, it MUST supply a first transition at the start point and MUST make time type 0 a placeholder meaning local time is unspecified, so the reader knows the file was cut. Leap-second records governing times inside the range are kept even if they begin earlier. When truncating the end, it MUST supply a last transition at the end point, an empty TZ string and a placeholder last time type. Clients SHOULD NOT use a truncated file for timestamps outside its range.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server hands out these files over the network, it labels each one with a registered media type that says whether leap seconds are included. If the server only has part of a zone's history, it marks the missing parts as unknown rather than guessing, and the client should not ask about times outside the covered range.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The format contains no executable code and no extensible areas that could store such code. TZif does contain counted arrays of data elements, so all counts should be checked when processing a file, to guard against references past the end of the object.

TZif provides no confidentiality or integrity protection of its own. Time zone information is normally public, but it is used in critical applications, so integrity protection may be required and must be provided externally. Data transmitted over a public channel MUST be protected with a layer such as TLS (RFC 8446): tampering can harm calendaring and scheduling operations, and the mere act of fetching a zone can leak the past, current or future location of a device or user.

Time zone designations are limited to ASCII alphanumerics, "-" and "+", which avoids confusion and encourages portability. Substituting localized abbreviations is the reader's responsibility; the RFC points to the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR) project as one approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The file itself cannot run code, but a damaged or altered file can still mislead programs, so readers should check the counts and transport should be encrypted. Fetching a time zone can also reveal where a device is, which is another reason to encrypt the connection.

viz.caption: THE SIX COUNT FIELDS IN THE TZIF HEADER

items.label: UT/local indicators
items.desc: Zero, or equal to typecnt. Says whether transition times were written as UT or local time.

items.label: standard/wall indicators
items.desc: Zero, or equal to typecnt. Says whether transition times were written as standard or wall-clock time.

items.label: leap-second records
items.desc: How many leap-second occurrence/correction pairs follow. Zero means no leap-second data.

items.label: transition times
items.desc: How many moments when the local-time rules change are listed.

items.label: local time type records
items.desc: How many clock styles (offset, DST flag, abbreviation). Must not be zero.

items.label: designation octets
items.desc: Total octets in the NUL-terminated abbreviation strings, including the final NUL. Must not be zero.

cells: 4 octets in the v1 block; 8 octets (64-bit) in the v2+ block
